title: Checkpoint: Algorithms That Choose
objective: After this level you can explain how routes, recommendations, feeds, ads and filters are chosen for you, and who can check them.
summary: One evening, six choosers: each optimizes a number, from travel time to a bid; change the number and you change the choice, which is why feedback loops and audits matter.

cards.headline: One evening, six algorithms choose for you.
cards.body: Chapter 8 finale. You drive home, book a ride for later, open a video app, scroll your feed, load a news page and check your email. At every step, software picked something for you. The question: picked by what rule, and aiming at what?

items.label: Getting around
points: Route finder: smallest total travel time
Ride app: lowest average wait across a batch

items.label: What you see
points: Recommender: what people with similar taste liked
Feed: a score built from predicted reactions

items.label: Behind the page
points: Ad auction: the highest bid that arrives in time
Spam filter: word counts turned into a spam probability

cards.headline: Change the number, change the choice
cards.body: Each chooser chases a number: minutes, wait time, predicted reactions, a bid, a probability. Swap the number and the same machinery picks something else. And the choices feed back: a recommender learns from clicks it helped cause. That's why checking matters. Auditors can test a system from outside with chosen inputs, and in the EU the GDPR limits significant decisions made solely by a machine.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 complete
learned: How route finders, feeds, recommenders, ad auctions and spam filters each choose by chasing a number.
Why a recommender can shape the very clicks it later learns from.
How ride apps match in batches, and why prices surge when requests outnumber drivers.
How audits and laws like the GDPR let people test and challenge automated decisions.

questions.prompt: In this chapter's evening, which chooser ranks things by a score built from predicted reactions?

options.label: The route finder
The ad auction
options.rationale: It picks the highest bid in time.

options.label: The social feed
The spam filter
options.rationale: It scores word counts as a spam probability.

questions.explanation: Feeds combine predictions about your reactions into a relevance score and sort by it.

questions.prompt: Why does it matter which number an algorithm is built to chase?

options.label: The number decides what gets chosen for you
The number sets how fast your phone runs
options.rationale: It sets the goal, not the hardware speed.

options.label: Only the number's size matters, not what it measures
options.rationale: What it measures is the whole point.

options.label: Numbers only matter to ad auctions
options.rationale: Every chooser in the chapter chases one.

questions.explanation: Swap the number, from travel time to predicted reactions to a bid, and the same machinery picks something else.

questions.prompt: Level 71's route finder and Level 74's ad auction both pick a winner by a number. What does each pick?

options.label: Both pick whatever arrived first
options.rationale: Neither goes by arrival order alone.

options.label: The route with the smallest total time; the highest bid in time
The route through the most roads; the lowest bid that arrives
options.rationale: Smallest total weight wins routes; highest bid wins ads.

options.label: The newest route; the most popular ad
options.rationale: Neither uses newness or popularity as its number.

questions.explanation: Route finding minimizes the total weight, such as travel time; the auction takes the highest bid that beats the deadline.

questions.prompt: From Level 71: when Dijkstra's search picks its next place, what does it compare?

options.label: Each place's known distance from the start
Each place's straight-line distance to the goal
options.rationale: It compares distances from the start.

options.label: How many roads meet at each place
Each place's name, alphabetically
options.rationale: It picks by smallest known distance.

questions.explanation: It picks the unvisited place with the smallest known distance from the start.

questions.prompt: From Level 78: in the 2006 music experiment, what could people in the social worlds see that the other group couldn't?

options.label: The bands' photos
How often each song had been downloaded in their world
Which songs music critics had already reviewed
The songs' lyrics
options.rationale: The extra information was download counts.

questions.explanation: People in each of the eight social worlds saw their own world's download counts.
